title: IDisposable, finalization and deterministic cleanup
description: Learn the Dispose pattern, how finalizers work as a safety net, and how SafeHandle wraps unmanaged resources reliably.

data.text: C# classes that wrap unmanaged resources — file handles, database connections, network sockets, native memory — must release those resources when they are no longer needed. The CLR's garbage collector only manages managed memory. It does not know about operating-system handles or native allocations. If you rely on the GC alone, those resources will stay open until the finalizer thread gets around to cleaning them up — which could be seconds or minutes later. `IDisposable` gives you a way to clean up deterministically: you decide exactly when the resource is released, not the runtime.

The `IDisposable` interface has a single method: `Dispose()`. When you call `Dispose()`, you are telling the object: I am done with you, release everything you hold now. The canonical pattern wraps `Dispose` with a finalizer as a safety net. If the consumer forgets to call `Dispose`, the finalizer runs eventually and releases the unmanaged resource. But finalizers are unpredictable — they run on a separate thread, they may not run at all if the process terminates abruptly, and they delay garbage collection by one extra cycle.

The standard Dispose pattern uses a boolean `disposing` parameter to distinguish between explicit cleanup and finalizer cleanup. When `disposing` is `true`, the call came from `Dispose()` or the `using` statement — you should release both managed and unmanaged resources. When `disposing` is `false`, the call came from the finalizer — you should release only unmanaged resources, because managed objects may already be finalized.

data.title: Implementing the Dispose pattern

data.text: `SafeHandle` is an abstract class in `Microsoft.Win32.SafeHandles` designed specifically to wrap operating-system handles. It is preferable to manually writing finalizers because the runtime guarantees that `SafeHandle` finalizers run even during AppDomain unloads or constrained execution regions. `SafeHandle` also supports reference counting for handles shared across multiple objects. The most common subclasses are `SafeFileHandle`, `SafeWaitHandle`, and `SafeMemoryMappedFileHandle`.

data.text: Finalizers: the safety net you do not want to rely on

A finalizer (`~ClassName()`) is a method the GC calls before reclaiming an object's memory. It runs on the finalizer thread, not your application thread. Objects with finalizers survive at least one full GC cycle because the runtime moves them to the finalization queue first. This delays memory reclamation. If the finalizer thread falls behind — for example, because many objects were finalized at once — you may see high memory usage even when the GC has identified the objects as unreachable.

items: Finalizers run on a dedicated thread; exceptions in finalizers terminate the process in .NET 2.0+.
Objects with finalizers are promoted to generation 2, increasing full GC pressure.
`GC.SuppressFinalization(this)` in `Dispose()` prevents the finalizer from running if cleanup is done early.
Never reference managed objects in a finalizer — they may already be finalized.

data.title: Critical finalizers and CERs are advanced techniques
data.text: `CriticalFinalizerObject` and constrained execution regions (CERs) guarantee that a finalizer runs even during resource constraints or AppDomain unloads. They are used internally by `SafeHandle` and are rarely needed in application code. Misusing CERs can cause hangs and deadlocks because the runtime pre-allocates resources for them. Prefer `SafeHandle` and `IDisposable` over raw critical finalizers.

data.title: Key takeaways
items: `IDisposable` provides deterministic cleanup; `using` ensures `Dispose()` runs even when exceptions occur.
Finalizers are a safety net, not a primary cleanup mechanism — they are slow and unpredictable.
`SafeHandle` is the preferred way to wrap OS handles; it avoids manual finalizer bugs.
Always call `GC.SuppressFinalization(this)` in `Dispose()` so the finalizer does not run after cleanup.
